reading.intro: Max once spent a year in Cologne, and he has told everyone about its cathedral ever since. Now Maya has brought him up the tower in Ulm: 768 steps, and a narrow stair. Halfway up, they meet a man who is coming down.
reading.photos[0].caption: Im Münster: sehr hoch, sehr kühl, sehr still.
reading.photos[1].caption: Die Treppe im Turm: Sie ist länger als dein Tag.
reading.en: Max: Another two hundred steps? Cologne Cathedral is much nicer. And bigger. · Mann: Bigger? This tower is higher! A hundred and sixty-one metres! Cologne Cathedral only has a hundred and fifty-seven. · Max: But Cologne has two towers. · Mann: Yes, because one wasn’t enough. · Maya: Which is older? · Mann: Cologne started earlier. But Ulm was finished quicker. Four years! That’s what they say in Ulm, anyway. · At the top. The town is small, the wind is strong, and Max can’t speak any more. · Maya: Well? Is that as nice as Cologne? · Max: It’s … just as high … as a heart attack. · Maya: Which house is that down there, the little one? · Max: That one? That’s the café. There’s cake there. It’s better than any tower. · A child comes up the last flight, not tired at all. · Kind: Daddy, the towers in Cologne were higher, though. · Maya: Come on, Max. Let’s go, before the man hears that.
reading.fact: Ulm’s minster tower is 161.5 metres, and it only reached that height in 1890, after building had stopped for three hundred years. The town’s other pride is a sparrow on the roof: the *Ulmer Spatz*, who taught its builders to carry a beam lengthways through the gate.

document.intro: A real board at the Kyffhäuser monument in Thuringia, in two languages. This is German you can compare: who pays more, when it opens later, which ticket is the better deal.
document.fact: Almost every German tower and monument charges a small fee for going up, and many have a price for *Azubis*, apprentices. Ask at the till: *Gibt es eine Ermäßigung?* It is a long word that saves a lot of money.
